claim: The small icons are a linear-light area average of the 96px mark, not a default resize
where_it_appears: favicon.ico (16/32/48) and favicon-48.png; generated by scripts/build-favicons.py
evidence_source: Owner asked 2026-09-06 whether the image quality could be improved. Checked for a better master first: there is no vector logo in the repository, and of the four 512px rasters, icon-512.png carries the symbol at the largest scale (logo.png is the lockup with the wordmark, so its symbol is smaller; assets/logo-BJ1TOn9V.png is palette-quantised to 120 colours in the crop region against icon-512.png's 2569). So 96 real pixels is the ceiling, and the quality loss was in the resampling rather than the source. An sRGB value is a perceptual encoding, not a quantity of light, so averaging those codes - the default in every image tool - averages the wrong thing and the white highlight on the olive comes out grey. Three methods were rendered at 16/32/48 and compared: sRGB Lanczos (current), linear-light Lanczos, and linear-light area average. Linear Lanczos was rejected outright - its negative lobes ring on edges this hard and put a black fringe around the olive at 48px that is nowhere in the source, with the darkest pixel landing at luminance 0. The area average cannot overshoot, and because 96 divides exactly by 16, 32 and 48 each output pixel is one whole n-by-n block, so it is not an approximation of the correct answer but the correct answer. Verified end to end: all three images inside the .ico match the generator's output exactly (max channel difference 0) and differ from a naive sRGB Lanczos by up to 47 levels. scripts/check-favicons.js recomputes the average and fails if any shipped icon is more than 1 level off; a default resize scores 38 and fails. NOTE: an earlier measurement in this session appeared to show linear-light performing worse at 32 and 48px - that metric used a box average as its reference and so was only measuring how much each filter rings, not which looked better. It was discarded rather than reported.

Enforced by scripts/check-generator-parity.js, now covering both generators and 17 pages, and comparing every file each one writes at whatever depth - which is what brought the /resources hub page inside the check rather than leaving it skipped. Proven by three negative tests: a one-word change to the template failed on six pages, a one-character edit to a shipped page failed on that page, and the same edit to the hub failed on the hub. NOTED WHILE DOING IT: the C-91 retired-tagline rule fires on prose about the rule. Both new docstrings originally quoted the retired wording to explain the defect and failed the suite for it. They now describe it and point at C-91 instead, which keeps the rule absolute rather than carving out an exemption for comments. RESOLVED BY RETIREMENT 2026-09-19, on the owner's instruction, after checking what used it. NOTHING RAN IT: Netlify's only build command is node scripts/build-geo.js; there is no .github/workflows directory at all; no npm script, Makefile, shell script or runbook invoked it; and the sole executor was the parity check added the same day to guard it. Meanwhile the seven pages it claimed to own had been edited by hand in 33 commits since it was written - the 220 kg barrel correction, the retired export-markets stat, the header social button, the new tagline, the logo dimensions - and from 2026-09-01 it could not have produced any of them, because the scratchpad read made it unrunnable outside the container that wrote those files. It was therefore dead code holding a second copy of pages somebody does edit, and the parity check made that visible without making it untrue. The script is deleted, its entry removed from scripts/check-generator-parity.js (now 10 pages, the product generator alone), and all nine /resources pages verified byte-identical by sha256 before and after: deleting a generator must not change a published page, and it did not. TWO CONSEQUENCES, NAMED AND ACCEPTED BY THE OWNER: nothing in the repository can now rebuild /resources from scratch, which matches the practice rather than changing it; and check-identity-strings.js and check-packaging-claims.js have one fewer generator to scan, which costs nothing, since both still scan the shipped pages, where a false claim would actually appear. A PREMISE CORRECTED IN PASSING: the alternative considered was reworking the script to read each page's own body from disk at generation time, described as the approach already used for the /ar/catalog reuse of product-page data. No such mechanism exists. The site has no HTML build step - Netlify's build command fetches a GeoLite2 database - and nothing under scripts/ or netlify/ reads a page's main element from disk. The /ar/catalog spec panels were editorial reuse of already-approved Arabic wording under Operating Rule 2, not a build-time mechanism, so that path would have been new work rather than a pattern followed.

claim: No committed file that can run or configure anything names a filesystem path on somebody machine
where_it_appears: 208 runnable tracked files - .js, .py, .sh, .json, .toml, .yml, .html, .css
evidence_source: Added 2026-09-19 on the owner instruction, after the defect behind C-95 and a sweep of both repositories. WHY IT EXISTS: generate-resource-pages.py read its header and footer from an absolute path in an ephemeral per-session scratchpad directory outside the repository. It survived eighteen days and nothing caught it - the suite did not run the script, so the broken read never executed, and nothing else ran it either. It was found by running the generator to check something unrelated and confirmed by reading its first fifteen lines. That is luck, not a discovery method. SWEEP RESULT, both repositories clean: umami-olivesegypt has no commit by the owner or by me (authors are the upstream umami maintainers), no scratchpad reference and no absolute host path, so the defect could not have reached it; olivesegypt-site retains the path only as elided prose in C-95, the Deploy 16 entry and one check docstring, and every one of the 22 file reads in scripts/ and netlify/ builds its path from ROOT, __dirname, path.resolve(__dirname, ...) or a walk of the repository. WHAT IS FLAGGED: /home/, /root/, /tmp/, /Users/, /var/folders/, /private/var/ and Windows drive paths in backslash form. WHAT IS NOT, AND WHY: web-absolute paths are URLs and the whole site is built from them; documentation is not scanned, because the deployment record quotes the original two lines verbatim and a path in a markdown file cannot be executed; and C:/ is not flagged because it cannot be told apart from an ordinary label:/path - the first draft flagged mailto:/, purged:/ and a CSS left:/ inside a regex. PROSE INSIDE A SCANNED FILE IS NOT EXEMPT. The one candidate for an exemption, a comment in check-generator-parity.js, was reworded to describe the path instead of quoting it, the same way the C-91 tagline rule was honoured rather than carved out. The allowlist is therefore empty, which is the intended state: a rule with an exemption for comments is one anybody routes around by writing a comment. THE POINT, asserted as its own test so it cannot quietly stop being true: asking the operating system for a temporary directory at run time is correct and stays correct everywhere. check-generator-parity.js does that three lines from a comment about this defect, and the check fails if it stops. The fault was never using a temporary directory; it was writing one machine answer into a file. PROVEN BY FIVE NEGATIVE TESTS, all exit 1: the original defect reintroduced verbatim into the product generator; a /home/ path in netlify/functions/leads.js; a single-backslash Windows path in netlify.toml; a doubled-backslash Windows path in a package.json string; and os.tmpdir() replaced by a literal, which failed two tests at once. THE FOURTH FOUND A REAL GAP: the pattern first required exactly one backslash and let the doubled form through - which is how a Windows path is always written inside a JS or JSON string literal. It now accepts one or two, and that line is only correct because the negative test was written before the check was trusted.

claim: Every committed script parses, and every dependency it names exists - checked without executing any of them
where_it_appears: 78 scripts under scripts/ and netlify/, and the build command in netlify.toml
evidence_source: Added 2026-09-19 on the owner instruction, closing the gap Deploy 17 recorded: nothing checked whether runnable code is ever run. npm test executed the check scripts, git ls-files and generate-product-pages.py and required four helper modules, leaving nine scripts neither executed nor loaded by anything - admin-password.js, build-geo.js, crm-create-user.js, crm-seed.js, db-roundtrip-check.js, kpi-roundtrip-check.js, send-test-email.js, build-favicons.py and generate-export-catalog-pdf.js. build-geo.js was the one that mattered: Netlify runs it on every deploy and nothing local did, so a syntax error or a renamed dependency in it would have been found by a failed production build. Same shape as C-95 - code nobody runs until it matters. NOTHING IS EXECUTED, BY DESIGN RATHER THAN BY LIMITATION: several of these scripts send email, write to the database or download a GeoLite2 archive, so a smoke test that ran them would be worse than none. node --check and Python ast.parse read and parse without evaluating. The check covers 78 files rather than the nine, so the list cannot go stale. SIX ASSERTIONS: every .js parses as CommonJS; every .py parses; every relative require resolves to a file that exists; every package require is a Node builtin, declared in package.json, or named tooling-only; every third-party Python import is stdlib or named tooling-only; and the script netlify.toml names in its build command exists and is among those parsed - which is the highest-value line, since renaming build-geo.js without editing netlify.toml breaks every deploy and nothing else would notice. TWO UNDECLARED DEPENDENCIES FOUND AND NAMED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: generate-export-catalog-pdf.js requires playwright and build-favicons.py imports PIL, neither declared anywhere. Both are one-off asset builders a maintainer runs with the tool installed, never part of the Netlify build, and adding Playwright to devDependencies would make every production deploy install a browser toolchain to render two PDFs nobody regenerates on deploy. They are listed in TOOLING_ONLY keyed to the one file allowed to use them, so the same import anywhere else still fails. PROVEN BY SIX NEGATIVE TESTS, all exit 1 except the last: a syntax error in build-geo.js; a local module renamed out from under a require in netlify/functions/leads.js; an undeclared package added to build-geo.js; an undeclared Python import added to build-favicons.py; netlify.toml pointed at a script that does not exist, which failed two assertions at once; and the one that matters most - a writeFileSync side effect injected after the shebang of crm-seed.js, so the file still parsed cleanly. The check passed 8 of 8 and the sentinel file was NOT created, while a genuine require of the same file did create it. The first attempt at that test was worthless: the line was inserted before the shebang, which pushed #! to line 2 and made the file unparsable, so the check rejected it and the sentinel proved nothing. The control - showing the side effect fires when the file really is loaded - is what makes the claim mean anything. WHAT IT STILL DOES NOT CATCH, and stated in the docstring: a require built at run time from a variable, a module that throws on load, a wrong argument, a missing environment variable. Parsing is not running, and the scripts that cannot safely be run stay unrun. This narrows the gap Deploy 17 described rather than closing it.
